title: Designing a payment system

facts.text: A payment system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems it can have.
When a user clicks the Buy button, a payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores the payment event in the database.

One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout; the payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order.
The payment executor stores the payment order, then calls an external PSP, a third-party intermediary with connections to acquiring banks and card networks, to finish the credit card payment.
A card payment goes through the processor and card association to the issuing bank, which approves or denies with a response code; the round trip typically takes 2–3 seconds.
Once the payment succeeds, the payment service updates the wallet with how much the seller holds, then calls the ledger service, which appends the new ledger information to the database.

The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping: each transaction is recorded as equal and opposite debit and credit entries so debits equal credits, which keeps records accurate and lets errors or fraud be detected.
For a $200 watch paid through PayPal, the e-commerce site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.
Exactly-once becomes easier when split in two: at-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check.

An idempotency key, usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, goes in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key; checking and recording the key must be atomic, for example with a unique constraint or Redis SET NX.
When the PSP call fails on a network error or timeout, the client retries the payment, which may succeed at a later attempt; the idempotency key stops the retry from charging twice.
Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files holding the bank account balance and the day's transactions; for cards, authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days.

Reconciliation compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match: a layer transforms different formats into one, and big data processing handles volume, Flink for near real-time or end-of-day batch such as Hadoop.

A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off; it is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches.
A reconciliation system is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.
The PSP must follow PCI DSS at one of four compliance levels set by annual transaction volume, and gateways screen orders for fraud before authorization.

notes: thin: no source sentence gives transaction volumes or estimates, a table-level data model, or an API beyond the idempotency-key header; wallet and ledger consistency is described only as two service calls.

title: Payment reconciliation

definition.text: The process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other.

facts.text: In double-entry bookkeeping a $200 PayPal purchase appears as a $200 order at the e-commerce site, a $200 PayPal transaction, and in the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.
Records in different systems come in different formats, such as the timestamp "2022/01/01" in one and "Jan 1, 2022" in another; a layer that transforms them into the same format solves it.
Massive data volume is handled with big data processing: a streaming platform such as Flink for near real-time reconciliation, or end-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop.
With a daily cut-off of 00:00:00, a record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy.
Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records; if a match is found the break is cleared and no more action is needed.
Even with exactly-once semantics a reconciliation system is always necessary, because there are many places that can go wrong; it is a safety net.

definition.text: A bookkeeping method in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries, debits and credits, so the books balance.

facts.text: Its purpose is to keep financial records accurate and allow errors or fraud to be detected.
It rests on the accounting equation, and every recorded transaction keeps that equation in balance.
Each transaction is entered in at least two ledger accounts so that total debits equal total credits, which is a partial check that every transaction was recorded correctly.
A debit entry is a transfer of value to an account and a credit entry a transfer from it; each transaction is a debit in one account and a credit in a second.
Each account type has a normal balance set by whether a debit or a credit increases it: a debit increases an asset, while a credit increases a liability.
Daybooks or journals serve as preliminary records and are totalled before posting to the nominal ledger, which limits ledger entries and ensures the integrity of the resulting financial information.
As transaction volume and complexity grow, companies use ledgers and accounting information systems to automate tracking of individual transactions.

definition.text: A third-party company that lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments.

facts.text: A PSP acts as an intermediary between consumers who pay and retailers who accept payment, and often also acts as a payment gateway or payment processor.

PSPs set up technical connections with acquiring banks and card networks, so merchants accept different payment methods without partnering with one bank, and the PSP manages processing and external network relationships.

Beyond processing, a PSP may offer risk management, transaction payment matching, digital wallets, reporting, fund remittance, currency exchange and fraud protection, and supplies software to integrate with e-commerce sites or point of sale systems.
PSP fees are typically charged as a percentage of each transaction or as a fixed cost per transaction.
The merchant remains responsible for data protection and must make sure the chosen provider observes the guidelines; compliance with PCI DSS is important.

A PSP must follow one of four PCI compliance levels set by annual transaction volume: Level 1 over 6 million, Level 2 between 1 and 6 million, Level 3 between 20,000 and 1 million, Level 4 under 20,000.

definition.text: A merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores.

facts.text: A gateway passes payment information between a payment portal, such as a website, mobile phone or interactive voice response service, and the front end processor or acquiring bank.
The gateway is not directly involved in the money flow; typically it is a web server to which the merchant's website or POS system is connected.
One gateway often connects several acquiring banks and payment methods under one system.
A gateway may let transaction data go straight from the customer's browser to the gateway, bypassing the merchant's systems, using a redirect or an iframe.

Many gateways screen orders for fraud and calculate tax in real time before the authorization request goes to the processor, using geolocation, velocity pattern analysis, deny-list lookups, delivery address verification and basic AVS checks.
A bank or a specialised provider such as a PSP can supply a gateway, and white label gateways let PSPs, e-commerce platforms or acquiring banks brand the technology as their own.

definition.text: The steps by which a card payment is authorized by the issuing bank, then cleared and settled so the merchant's acquiring bank is funded.

facts.text: The merchant forwards the transaction details to the gateway, which converts the message from XML to ISO 8583 or a variant and passes it to the processor used by the merchant's acquiring bank.
The processor forwards the details to the card association, such as Visa or Mastercard, which may act as the issuing bank or route the transaction to the correct card issuing bank.

The issuing bank approves or denies with a response code and a failure reason; the answer returns through the processor and gateway to the website in typically 2–3 seconds, and the issuer holds an authorization for the approved amount.
After the merchant fulfills the order, the process repeats to clear the authorization, which moves the issuing bank's auth-hold to a debit and prepares settlement with the acquiring bank.
At the end of the day the merchant submits its approved authorizations as a batch to its acquiring bank via its processor, and the acquiring bank makes a batch settlement request of the card issuer.

The issuer pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day, and the acquiring bank deposits the approved funds into the merchant's account the same or next day; authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days.

definition.text: A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value.

facts.text: Modern electronic payment systems move money between bank accounts without bank staff intervening, using cash substitutes such as debit and credit cards, electronic funds transfers, direct credits and debits and internet banking.

An automated clearing house processes transactions in batches and is a net settlement system, so settlement may be delayed, which poses settlement risk; it is typically used for low-value, non-urgent transactions.

Real-time gross settlement settles each transaction as soon as it is processed, one to one without netting, and payments are final and irrevocable; it is typically used for high-value, urgent transactions.
Instant payment systems typically run 24x7x365 and complete a transfer from debit of the payer's account to credit of the beneficiary's within 10–15 seconds.
